newsitem.title: USA: Weak durable goods seen no threat to U.S. growth.
newsitem.headline: Weak durable goods seen no threat to U.S. growth.

text.p: Despite a surprising decline in durable goods orders for May, the U.S. economy continues to sail along at a healthy clip, economists said.
Durable goods orders fell 0.6 percent last month, compared with expectations for a 0.6 percent increase.
"It didn't give us much insight," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc. There was some slowing overall but capital orders were up, he said.
"It was a moderate report and is not going to change anyone's views" on the economy, Glassman said.

Virtually all analysts have now ruled out a tightening of monetary policy by the Federal Reserve at its policy-making meeting in July, and many now doubt the central bank will raise interest rates at its August meeting.
"My sense is that the consumer has pulled back somewhat but business spending still looks good," Glassman said.
The durable goods data are known to be volatile and the markets treat the figures with some trepidation, he said.

Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc, said, "You have to be careful with this number as it is volatile. But with that caveat, it represents one more piece of evidence that the economy is cooling in the second quarter."
Moran said underlying trends in the economy remain strong, but with recent signs of slowing, the Federal Reserve probably would be wise to refrain from tightening in July.

"We were a little bit surprised (by the durable goods data). but this is a fairly volatile series and we're not inclined to read a great deal into it," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
Resler said capital goods orders seemed to be moderating and shipments showed the first drop since December.
"But all in all, it's dangerous to read too much into one month's movement," he said.
